content.instructions: Use the fraction circles or drawings below to complete the worksheet. Label each part as 'numerator' or 'denominator'. Draw and label your own fractions to show equal parts.
items: Circle the numerator in 2/4 and underline the denominator. Explain what each number means in 1-2 sentences.
Draw a circle divided into 3 equal parts. Shade 2 parts and write the fraction: _______/_______
Label the shaded part of this rectangle as a fraction. Is the shaded part more than, less than, or equal to 1/2? Explain.
Create your own fraction drawing: Divide a shape into ______ equal parts. Shade ______ parts. Write the fraction: _______/_______
answer_key: Numerator = 2 (parts we have), Denominator = 4 (total parts). Example explanation: Numerator shows how many parts are shaded, denominator shows how many equal parts make the whole.
Drawing of 3-part circle with 2 shaded. Fraction: 2/3
Drawing of rectangle with 3/4 shaded. Answer: More than 1/2 (since 3/4 = 0.75 > 0.5).
Student-created drawing with correct labeling. Fraction format: [number]/[total parts]

content.instructions: Use whiteboard markers to complete these fraction scaling exercises. Label all numerators (top numbers) in red and denominators (bottom numbers) in blue. Explain in 1-2 words why both numbers change when scaling.
items: Draw 1/2 and 2/4 on whiteboard: circle top as numerator (red) and box bottom as denominator (blue).
Scale 1/3 to 2/6: show how numerator (1→2) and denominator (3→6) both multiply by 2.
Create your own example: scale 1/4 to 3/12. Label and explain the pattern.
Compare 1/2 vs 2/4: use arrows to show how the fraction bar grows and label parts.
answer_key: 1/2 (red numerator) and 2/4 (red numerator) with blue denominators; scaling doubles both parts
Numerator 1×2=2, denominator 3×2=6; scaling factor of 2 maintains equivalence
Numerator 1×3=3, denominator 4×3=12; scaling factor of 3 preserves value
Arrows show fraction bar length doubles; numerator and denominator both increase proportionally
